sources: Alaska Department of Fish and Game, Alaska Fish & Wildlife News (Jan 2020): more people are injured in Alaska by moose than by bears; moose can deliver dangerous blows with their hooves when threatened; https://www.adfg.alaska.gov/index.cfm?adfg=wildlifenews.view_article&articles_id=939

National Wildlife Federation, Moose: largest deer, about six feet tall at the shoulder; excellent swimmers that can hold their breath underwater for 30 seconds; can run over 35 mph; antlers up to six feet across; females protect calves with kicks that can break bones; https://www.nwf.org/Educational-Resources/Wildlife-Guide/Mammals/Moose

National Park Service, Moose: Did You Know?: largest bull at the Kenai Moose Research Station weighed 1,697 lb; mature moose grow about an inch of antler a day; antlers up to 75 lb; tested down to -22 F without feeling cold; https://www.nps.gov/articles/moose-did-you-know.htm
National Park Service, Isle Royale: Moose: in summer moose feed in lakes and beaver ponds on aquatic plants that grow beneath the surface; https://www.nps.gov/isro/learn/nature/moose.htm
National Park Service, Yellowstone: Moose: bulls shed antlers in winter and grow new ones each spring; https://www.nps.gov/yell/learn/nature/moose.htm

North Dakota Game and Fish, Winter Ticks and Moose: in good tick years 75,000 to 150,000 winter ticks on a single moose; infested moose rub off much of their hair, looking grey ('ghost moose'); https://gf.nd.gov/wildlife-notes/winter-ticks-and-moose

beats.say: In Alaska, a moose is more likely to hurt you than a bear is.
The moose. The biggest deer on Earth. Six feet tall at the shoulder.
The biggest one ever weighed at an Alaska research station was nearly seventeen hundred pounds.
And it can run over thirty-five miles an hour.
A mother moose kicks hard enough to break bones.
Most of the time, though, it just wants to eat.
